title: Stevia: What It Is, Where It Comes From, and Why Stevia Products Are Not All the Same

seo.title: Stevia: What It Is and Why Products Taste So Different
seo.meta_description: Stevia rebaudiana leaves contain intensely sweet steviol glycosides. Commercial products usually use purified glycosides and often blend them with erythritol, dextrose, or fibers. Reb A, Reb M, and other glycosides also taste different.
seo.search_intent: Understand what stevia is, which compounds actually sweeten foods, why different stevia products have different ingredients and tastes, and how the ADI and U.S. regulatory distinction should be interpreted.

excerpt: “Stevia” can mean a plant, purified steviol glycosides, or a tabletop product containing only a tiny amount of those glycosides blended with erythritol, dextrose, maltodextrin, or fiber. High-purity steviol glycosides are roughly 200–400 times sweeter than sucrose, so very little is needed. Reb A, Reb D, Reb M, stevioside, and other glycosides also have different sweetness and aftertaste profiles.
content_html:
“Stevia” is not one single ingredient. The word can refer to the Stevia rebaudiana plant, its leaves, purified steviol glycosides, or a tabletop product that contains a tiny amount of those glycosides blended with erythritol, dextrose, maltodextrin, or fiber.

The distinction matters because steviol glycosides are high-intensity sweeteners. FDA describes them as roughly 200–400 times sweeter than table sugar, so pure glycosides would be impractical to measure with an ordinary teaspoon.

The sweetness comes from specific glycosides in the leaf

Stevia leaves contain a family of molecules built around steviol with different sugar groups attached. They include stevioside and rebaudiosides A, D, and M, among many others.

They do not taste identical. Reb A can produce a more noticeable bitter or licorice-like aftertaste, while Reb D and Reb M have shown different sensory profiles and, in some studies, greater consumer acceptance.

Two foods labeled “sweetened with stevia” can therefore taste noticeably different even when neither contains sugar.

Food companies do not simply grind whole stevia leaves into everything

In the United States, FDA has reviewed numerous GRAS notices for high-purity steviol glycosides, generally at least 95% purity. These include Reb A, stevioside, Reb D, and mixtures of glycosides.

Whole stevia leaf and crude stevia extracts are different. FDA does not consider those forms GRAS for use as sweeteners, and they are not permitted as sweetening ingredients under the same framework.

The European Union likewise regulates specific E 960 steviol-glycoside categories, including leaf-derived and certain enzymatically produced forms. “From a plant” and “authorized purified sweetener” are therefore not interchangeable concepts.

Why a stevia packet can be mostly erythritol or dextrose

A sweetener hundreds of times sweeter than sugar needs bulk if consumers are expected to use a spoon or packet. Manufacturers dilute the intense sweetener with a carrier that improves dosing, flow, mouthfeel, and teaspoon equivalence.

Erythritol can provide bulk with very little usable energy. Dextrose and maltodextrin provide carbohydrate and some calories. Soluble fibers can serve yet another technological role.

This means two “stevia” tabletop products can differ in calories, carbohydrate, digestive tolerance, and sweetness per teaspoon because most of the powder may not be steviol glycosides at all.

The ADI is expressed as steviol equivalents

EFSA established an Acceptable Daily Intake of 4 mg/kg body weight per day expressed as steviol equivalents. For a 154-lb (70-kg) person, that corresponds to 280 mg steviol equivalents per day.

That is not the same as 280 mg of every commercial stevia blend. Different glycosides have different molecular weights, and tabletop powders contain carriers, so the actual formulation matters.

An ADI is a lifetime safety reference, not a recommended minimum intake.

“Zero calorie” depends on the whole product

The steviol glycosides themselves are used at such tiny quantities that their energy contribution is negligible. The carrier can change the label.

An erythritol-based blend may still contribute virtually no usable energy, while dextrose or maltodextrin adds some carbohydrate and calories. Small serving sizes can also affect how numbers round on labels.

In a finished food, replacing sugar may require extra starch, fat, fiber, or water-management ingredients, so a “stevia-sweetened” claim does not predict the final calorie count by itself.

WHO's non-sugar-sweetener guidance is not a toxicity declaration

WHO's 2023 guideline includes stevia and stevia derivatives among non-sugar sweeteners and recommends against relying on NSS for long-term weight control or prevention of chronic disease.

WHO explicitly states that the recommendation is not a toxicological reassessment and does not replace safety limits established by food-safety bodies. The recommendation is conditional and addresses long-term dietary strategy, not a claim that approved steviol glycosides are poisonous.

How to compare two stevia products

Read the entire ingredient list first. Look for erythritol, dextrose, maltodextrin, or another bulking ingredient. Then compare calories, carbohydrate, and serving size.

If taste is the issue, the glycoside profile can also matter. Reb A, Reb M, and mixed-glycoside systems do not have identical sensory properties.

The practical rule: stevia is the plant, steviol glycosides are the regulated high-intensity sweeteners, and the supermarket product may be a much broader blend. Reading the ingredient list prevents treating all three as if they were the same thing.

faq.question: Is stevia a plant or a sweetener?
faq.answer: Both terms are used, but food sweeteners are usually purified steviol glycosides derived from stevia or produced through authorized processes.

faq.question: Why do stevia products contain erythritol?
faq.answer: Steviol glycosides are hundreds of times sweeter than sugar and need a bulking ingredient so consumers can measure them conveniently.

faq.question: Do all stevia glycosides taste the same?
faq.answer: No. Reb A, Reb D, Reb M, stevioside, and other glycosides differ in sweetness, bitterness, and aftertaste.
